prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: B052 is the only candidate that all eight of us ranked, and it is the one where scientific merit, clean attribution and maturity point the same way. Katori's magic-wavelength idea is a simple picture: choose the light wavelength at which the trapping light shifts both clock levels equally, so thousands of atoms can be held and interrogated without Doppler or recoil problems. Ye's group then showed that this could be pushed to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and to long coherence times. The consequence is measurement of gravitational redshift over millimetres, tests of the constancy of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches and a credible route to redefining the second. The result has been reproduced and compared by independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others), which is exactly the robustness I look for. It is a precision result that says something about nature, not merely a technological advance, and two names fit the three-person limit without strain.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation, raised by several colleagues, is that the metrology line already received the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize, so a lattice-clock prize may look like a sequel and may be read as instrument-building rather than a discovery. There is also a real attribution fringe: Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Yb and Hg lattice groups, and the ion-clock community (Al+ and others) could argue for credit. Because the physics is incremental in principle (the same atomic transitions, better control), the committee must be able to say precisely what is new, and I think the answer is the many-atom, Doppler-free, recoil-free interrogation scheme enabled by magic wavelengths, together with its demonstrated accuracy. I have not verified every priority date and rely on memory for some of them.

responses.point: Olsson notes that Ye used the frequency comb honoured in 2005 and that other lattice-clock groups are not on the list, and she ranks B052 only fourth. She also puts the aberration-corrected electron microscope first as a genuine invention.
responses.response: I accept that the comb overlap must be addressed in the citation, and I would word it around the lattice clock itself, not around the comb. The comb is a ruler that reads out an optical frequency, while the lattice clock is a new reference oscillator with its own physics (magic-wavelength trapping, many-atom interrogation, control of blackbody and collisional shifts). The two are complementary, and a prize to one does not exhaust the other. On B011, I defer to her expertise on the practical importance of aberration correction, but only one member ranked it, and she herself flags Krivanek and the STEM correctors as an unresolved attribution issue. For me that makes it less ready than B052, where two names are broadly uncontested.

responses.point: Danielsson puts the Higgs experiments first as the clearest discovery delivered by nature, while ranking optical lattice clocks fourth and asking whether metrology counts as a discovery or an instrument advance.
responses.response: I agree that the Higgs observation is a monumental result, and I do not rank it with ill will. But my difficulty is the one he himself writes: three founder-level names do not map onto the thousands who made the measurement, and Olsson and Mehlig say the same. A prize whose attribution we cannot defend is a weaker prize, however important the physics. On his question about metrology, I would say lattice clocks are a discovery in the sense that nobody expected a many-atom trap to be compatible with an atomic transition at the 1e-18 level; the magic wavelength is a result about atomic structure. I would welcome an organisation-based discussion of ATLAS and CMS if the Chair thinks the statutes permit it, but I do not think we can resolve it with B010 as framed.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B052 first as the clearest case of a new measurement technique changing what can be observed, and B035 second, while noting that atom interferometry overlaps with earlier prizes and that Chu is absent from the credit list.
responses.response: We agree on the first choice and the order of the top two, so I will concentrate on where I would qualify his view of B035. I like atom interferometry because it asks where quantum matter waves meet gravity, but the credit problem is serious: Chu already shared the 1997 prize and is the natural third name with Kasevich, which leaves Pritchard, Bordé and Mlynek-type early demonstrations in a delicate position. I would keep it as an alternative, not as a second part of a shared prize now. If we want a two-part configuration later, the clock plus atom interferometry would be coherent as precision quantum measurement, but I would want that to be driven by the attribution being resolved, not by our shared field.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and the lattice clock second, calls the clock physics clean and mature, and sees no serious dispute over principal credit, while asking whether cQED is distinct enough from the 2025 prize and flagging a possible conflict of his own.
responses.response: I welcome his agreement that the principal credit for B052 is not seriously disputed, which is the point on which I am most dependent on colleagues outside my narrow area. On circuit QED, I share his worry about timing: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits is close in subject, and the Blais versus Girvin theory question for a three-person split leaves a real attribution gap. I also thank him for stating his conflict candidly, and I would suggest the committee note it in our record. I do not think this makes cQED unprizeworthy, but I think it is a reason to wait, not a reason to put it ahead of B052 now.

responses.point: Eriksson puts topological insulators first as a verified new state of matter in real materials, and ranks lattice clocks fifth, as a clear metrological advance that some may see as precision engineering over new physics.
responses.response: His point that topological insulators are a verified new class of matter is fair and, as I wrote in my own opening, the concept is deep and confirmed. My difficulty is the one he lists himself: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan are outside the credit list, and the 2016 prize covered part of the topological line. On the 'precision engineering' charge, I would answer that the 1e-18 clock is not engineering for its own sake; it measures the gravitational redshift between two clocks separated by about a millimetre, which is quantum mechanics and general relativity in the same laboratory. I would ask him whether the topological insulator case can be restated with a defensible three-name set, because without that I cannot move it above B052.

responses.point: Pearce, our Chair, ranks IceCube first as combined instrumentation and discovery of a new window on the universe, and ranks the lattice clock third, saying it is outside his expertise and noting that Ye's overlap with the thorium clock needs care.
responses.response: I take his point about IceCube seriously: a new observational window delivered by a cubic-kilometre instrument is just the sort of discovery nature gives us, and the Halzen and Spiering credit is cleaner than for most large collaborations. My reservations are about maturity and attribution: the diffuse flux is established, but the source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are still at moderate significance, and the DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA pioneers are not in the list. On the thorium overlap, I would say that a lattice-clock prize to Ye does not preempt or double count a later nuclear-clock prize, since the citation would be restricted to the lattice clock; the committee can simply record that. I would ask him whether the neutrino community would regard the source results as timely now or a few years from now.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize.
Whether Katori and Ye adequately cover the priority record, given Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and the Yb, Hg and Al+ clock groups; I have not verified every priority date.
Whether atom interferometry (B035) can be given a defensible three-name set without Chu, and whether it could pair with B052 in a two-part prize.
Whether the IceCube source associations will have matured enough in the committee's judgement.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with the B052 candidates (Katori, Ye) is apparent from my profile: I have no recorded collaboration with either, and my collaborators (L'Huillier, Keller group, Dahlström, Argenti, Schuch, Indelicato) are not among them. For transparency, I am a long-time collaborator of the 2023 laureate Anne L'Huillier and work in atomic theory, which is adjacent to precision atomic metrology; Paul Indelicato works on precision atomic spectroscopy. None of these connections is with a credited name on any shortlisted ballot that I am putting forward, so I do not think recusal is needed.
